reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it presents technology developments and coronavirus-related information as technology news rather than offering a creator-owned financial or data-collection scheme. The websites, product promotion, and alcohol story are presented as reported misinformation or safety examples, with an explicit warning not to visit the websites. The closing request to subscribe is ordinary audience engagement and is not tied to payment, credentials, or financial participation.

many such fake websites have been created which are related to those named as, Corona Virus. So that you can go there to get the updates. But you won't get the updates. But will steal your data.
The Delhi police has told them to not visit such websites.

opening.argument: Judge the promised benefit and the requested action together. The headline leads with worldwide support worth ₹6000 Cr, while the narration says small businesses would receive help through advertising rather than direct payments. The video closes by asking viewers to subscribe and press the bell for future updates. That sequence uses a substantial benefit claim to attract attention, then converts interest in further updates into an action. The question is whether the apparent news format makes that solicitation seem more credible than it has earned.

if you want to know more updates like this Subscribe this channel if you have already done so and on the bell icon press the bell icon

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense is right that the narration calls the support advertising, not a cash payment. But that qualification makes the headline's large support figure especially important to scrutinize: a viewer drawn by the headline must listen further to learn what the help means. Nor does calling the closing request ordinary engagement resolve whether the benefit-led headline was used to secure that engagement. The absence of a payment request narrows the concern; it does not, by itself, explain the promise-and-action sequence.

citations.quote: Google Ceo Sundar Pichai Will Support ₹6000 Cr Worldwide
Its not like, that the money has been given directly.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The proposed linkage fails at the crucial point. The narrator explicitly says the support is not money given directly and describes advertising for small companies and NGOs. The only viewer action requested is subscribing for more updates. Nothing in those passages offers the viewer a reward for subscribing or a way to claim the headline's support. A prominent news headline followed by an ordinary subscription request does not establish a reward solicitation.

opening.argument: Several attention and destination signals appear in one presentation: a headline announcing ₹6000 Cr in worldwide support, social-media links in the description, and a passage saying coronavirus-themed websites promise updates but steal visitors' data. Those elements warrant a careful look at where the video directs attention. The dangerous sites are expressly described as deceptive; their presence makes destination and promised-content mismatches a concrete issue here, not a hypothetical one. The case for concern is the combination of a large benefit headline, reachable external channels, and discussion of data-taking sites, even though the narration does not say those channels are the sites it warns about.

So that you can go there to get the updates. But you won't get the updates. But will steal your data.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The warning not to visit the listed websites is strong evidence for the defense's reading of that segment. Still, it does not make the separate social-media links or the large support headline disappear. The judge should assess those elements on their own terms, while recognizing that the source does not identify the description's links as the harmful sites. The warning settles how the narrator presents the sites, but it does not answer every question raised by the video's other attention and destination cues.

Google Ceo Sundar Pichai Will Support ₹6000 Cr Worldwide

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The argument combines unrelated facts without establishing a deceptive path for viewers. The supplied links are identified as the creator's Instagram and Twitter accounts, while the narration says the coronavirus-themed sites steal data and relays a police warning not to visit them. No cited evidence connects those sites to the social accounts or asks viewers to submit information to claim support. The alarming destination is the subject of a warning, not a destination promoted to the audience.

opening.argument: The technology-news framing should not end the inquiry into what the presentation promotes. Its headline foregrounds substantial worldwide support; the narration discusses advertising help for small companies and NGOs; the description invites viewers to the creator's social accounts; and the closing asks them to subscribe for updates. Together, these passages can be read as using the support story to build an audience across the channel and its external accounts. The misinformation warnings may be sincere, but they do not erase that promotional function. A judge should examine whether the prominent support claim is doing more work as an audience-acquisition hook than as a carefully bounded report.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Describing the series as technology news addresses its stated format, but not whether its framing also serves promotion. The cited support story and requests to follow or subscribe give the video an audience-building function. The defense's strongest point remains that the website segment warns viewers away from the sites; that passage should not be treated as an invitation to visit them. The narrower issue is whether the support headline is used to attract participation in the creator's audience, despite the absence of a viewer claim process.

Google Ceo Sundar Pichai Will Support ₹6000 Cr Worldwide
The Delhi police has told them to not visit such websites.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Audience-building does not turn this report into a scam offer. The narrator specifies that the Google support concerns advertising for small companies and NGOs, not money handed to viewers. The closing asks for a subscription to receive more updates, with no promised cash, asset, claim process, or exchange for financial information. The video's discussion of deceptive websites also tells viewers not to visit them. The promotional reading identifies channel engagement, but not deceptive reward acquisition.
